articles.title: Shopify 2026-10 API: Metafield Fixes & Stable Lag Traps
articles.excerpt: The ownerType Trap in 2026-10 If you are migrating your app from the 2024-10 or 2025-01 API versions to 2026-10, you are likely hitting silent failures in your metafield synchronization logic. The 202…
articles.body: The ownerType Trap in 2026-10 If you are migrating your app from the 2024-10 or 2025-01 API versions to 2026-10 , you are likely hitting silent failures in your metafield synchronization logic. The 2026-10 release introduced a stricter enforcement of the ownerType field in the metafieldsSet and metafieldsDelete mutations. Previously, Shopify’s GraphQL API would infer the owner type based on the ID prefix (e.g., gid://shopify/Product/... ). In 2026-10 , this inference is deprecated for high-throughput apps and results in a 202 Accepted response that never actually commits the data if the inferred type conflicts with your app’s scope permissions. This is not a "soft" deprecation.

articles.excerpt: Most teams drop in coreos/go-oidc and call it done. That works until you hit a non-standard provider, a subtle validation bypass, or a token leakage bug you can't explain because you never read the sp…
articles.body: Most teams drop in coreos/go-oidc and call it done. That works until you hit a non-standard provider, a subtle validation bypass, or a token leakage bug you can't explain because you never read the spec. Building OIDC from scratch takes about 300 lines of Go — this article walks through every step. What the Authorization Code Flow Actually Does OIDC sits on top of OAuth 2.0 and adds identity. Where OAuth 2.0 handles authorization (can this client access this resource?), OIDC adds authentication: who is this user, and can I trust that claim?

articles.title: Never mark a crypto order paid twice: confirmations, reorgs and out-of-order webhooks
articles.excerpt: A classic crypto checkout bug goes like this. A webhook comes in, the shop marks the order paid, a retry of the same webhook arrives four seconds later, and a second fulfilment job goes into the queue…
articles.body: A classic crypto checkout bug goes like this. A webhook comes in, the shop marks the order paid, a retry of the same webhook arrives four seconds later, and a second fulfilment job goes into the queue. It's easy to write, easy to miss in testing, and it's a good reason to think properly about what "paid" means when the money moves on a blockchain. Card payments trained most of us to treat a payment as a single yes/no event. On-chain payments are messier. A transfer is seen, then it gathers confirmations, and once in a while the block it landed in disappears. Customers send too little, or too much, or pay again an hour after the invoice expired. Your webhook receiver has to make sense of all of that, often out of order. This post is about the order-system side of that problem.

articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine Exorcist: The Ghosts Hiding in Your Codebase 👻 It is late. You open a repository you have not touched in months. The feature works. The tests pass. The README looks fine. Then you notice a configuration file you do not remember adding. A dependency nobody seems to use. A scheduled job whose purpose has been lost to time. Somewhere in the repository, a secret might still be sitting in plain sight. Nothing is necessarily on fire. That is what makes these things easy to miss. Software accumulates history.

articles.title: A weekly housing-rules and mortgage-rate digest in one Python file
articles.excerpt: If you follow the property market, you know the routine: a ministry announces a change to energy-performance rules, a central bank publishes a lending survey, and you find out three weeks later. Check…
articles.body: If you follow the property market, you know the routine: a ministry announces a change to energy-performance rules, a central bank publishes a lending survey, and you find out three weeks later. Checking ten websites by hand is not a habit anyone keeps. I wrote a Hermes skill, real-estate-regulation-watch , that does the boring part. It reads public RSS feeds, keeps only the items matching housing and credit keywords (accents ignored), remembers what it already showed you in a small JSON file, and prints a Markdown digest where every line ends with its source URL. It also pulls the monthly cost of borrowing for French home loans from the ECB open data API. No API key, only the Python standard library.

Some fix bugs, some build the next step of an epic, and one or two do research or write tests. The agents got good enough that they stopped being the bottleneck. I became the bottleneck - which is quite popular slang in today's world if you even look at all these posts on LinkedIn, Reddit or other socials that include the software dev. articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 28, 1971: Britain launches its 1st satellite Prospero into space on a Black Arrow rocket
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 28, 1971, the United Kingdom launched its first satellite. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 28, 1971, the United Kingdom launched its first satellite. The satellite was named Prospero, but it was also known as the X-3. This wasn't Britain's first satellite , but it was the first and only one the British space program launched with one of its own rockets. The first six British satellites all launched from the United States on NASA rockets. Prospero launched on a carrier rocket called the Black Arrow. The Prospero mission was the fourth and final flight of a Black Arrow rocket . Prospero was designed to study how the environment in space affects communications satellites. It tested things solar cells and telemetry systems, and even had a micrometeoroid detector that would determine small particles in space posed a threat to the spacecraft.

articles.title: 5 days beneath the waves: What it's like to live in an underwater 'space station'
articles.excerpt: Confined inside a research station 22 feet (7 meters) underwater, Analog Astronaut Commander Dr. Musilova and her crew performed research and maintenance activities like future astronauts on Mars.
articles.body: Living underwater was surprisingly peaceful. It was in many ways exactly what I imagine living on Mars would be like one day. There were no humans around us, except for my three SEA STAR crewmembers and me. Apart from the human noises we made, we couldn't hear anything other than the life support systems keeping us alive submerged 22 feet (7 meters) below the surface. We were living in these extreme conditions to study the challenges astronauts may face on long-duration space missions. Since performing research in space is still rare and expensive, there are numerous facilities around the world that focus on recreating space-like conditions on Earth . One of those stations is the Jules' Undersea Lab, where the SEA STAR simulated space mission took place.

articles.title: ISS astronaut will conduct Canada's 1st spacewalk in 7 years on Oct. 29: Watch it live
articles.excerpt: Joshua Kutryk will venture outside the International Space Station on Oct. 29, on the first spacewalk by a Canadian astronaut in more than seven years. Here's how to watch it live.
articles.body: The next International Space Station (ISS) spacewalk will have more maple-leaf flavor than usual, as a Canadian astronaut will become the first to go outside the orbiting complex in seven years. Canadian Space Agency (CSA) astronaut Joshua Kutryk, who's also a colonel in the Royal Canadian Air Force, will help the ISS boost its power supply during his first-ever spacewalk on Thursday (Oct. 29). Kutryk will be joined by NASA astronaut Anil Menon, who has done three spacewalks already and also serves as a colonel with the U.S. Space Force . The duo are scheduled to venture outside the orbiting lab at 8 a.m. EDT (1200 GMT), kicking off a spacewalk that will last roughly 6 hours and 45 minutes. You can watch it live here at Space.com , courtesy of NASA, beginning at 6:30 a.m. EDT (1030 GMT).

articles.title: Meet Apeiron, Virgin Galactic's 1st 'Delta-class' space plane
articles.excerpt: Virgin Galactic has officially unveiled its first "Delta-class" space plane, and announced the results of the worldwide vote to choose its name.
articles.body: Virgin Galactic has officially unveiled the first space plane in its next-gen "Delta" line, and announced the results of the worldwide vote to choose its name. Spaceship Apeiron will be the first Delta-class vehicle, Virgin Galactic revealed on Wednesday (Oct. 28). Apeiron (pronounced "A'-per-on," according to the announcement) takes its name from the ancient Greek word meaning "boundless," and was selected through a public poll that drew votes from thousands of people across 83 countries and six continents. The reveal comes on the same day that the space plane is scheduled to be flown from its manufacturing facility in Mesa, Arizona, to Spaceport America in New Mexico, where the vehicle will undergo final preparations before beginning flight tests.

articles.excerpt: A U.S. military intelligence agency has released an incredible new photograph of China's secretive space plane, showing it docked to another spacecraft in orbit.
articles.body: A photograph of China's reusable Shenlong space plane docked to another spacecraft, taken by Vantor's WorldView 3 satellite from a distance of 56 miles (90 kilometers). (Image credit: Satellite image ©2026 Vantor) A U.S. military intelligence agency has released an incredible new photograph of China's secretive space plane, showing it docked to another spacecraft in orbit. The photograph was taken in 2024 by Vantor's WorldView 3 satellite, from a distance of 56 miles (90 kilometers). Ground-based observers have previously photographed Shenlong in orbit , but this new photo from Vantor, taken from space, reveals new details about the mysterious spacecraft in stunning clarity, with a resolution of 4.5 centimeters (1.8 inches) per pixel.

articles.title: The final ‘Dune: Part Three’ trailer reignites war on Arrakis and leaves us with more questions than answers
articles.excerpt: The spoilerific final look at Denis Villeneuve's third and final sci-fi epic is loaded with action and drama that set it apart from Dune: Messiah's pages.
articles.body: Dune: Part Three 's marketing campaign has been a long and generous one, but Warner Bros. and Legendary Pictures knew an extra push was needed in order to compete with Avengers: Doomsday , as both sci-fi blockbusters will be releasing next to each other at Christmas. In its final trailer, Denis Villeneuve's threequel goes all out. This isn't the first time a Dune: Part Three trailer has left us with more questions than answers , but the in-depth look at the character dynamics and plot beats that await will make longtime fans of Frank Herbert's works raise their eyebrows. Messiah, the second installment in the book series, is a novel of long monologues and very tense conversations.
